title: Design a URL shortener
dek: Zotato sends crores of promo SMS, and every link in them is a short one like zot.to/2Bi. Turn long URLs into short codes, send people to the right page in milliseconds, and never hand out the same code twice.

items: Two calls: create a short link, and open one. Opening happens about a hundred times more often, so the design is built around fast reads.
Codes come from a counter written in base 62 (0–9, a–z, A–Z). Each server takes a block of 1,000 numbers at a time, so codes never clash and the counter is rarely asked.
Store `code → long URL` in a database keyed by the code; keep hot codes in Redis, so most redirects never touch the database.
Answer with 302 if you want to count every click (the browser asks you each time), 301 if you'd rather the browser remember it.
Send clicks to a stream for analytics, so counting never slows a redirect.
A restaurant's marketing tool turns a long URL into a short one, optionally with a custom name (`zot.to/biryani50`) and an expiry date.
Anyone who opens the short link is sent to the long URL.
Out of scope here: user accounts, a dashboard, custom domains, and detailed analytics beyond counting clicks.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: 99.9% of redirects work; creating links can be slightly less available
A code always points to the URL it was made for; no two links share a code
10 crore new links a day, about 100 opens per link

items: Writes: 10 crore links a day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200 a second. One database handles that.
Reads: 100 opens per link ≈ 1.2 lakh redirects a second on average, about 3.5 lakh at peak. That needs a cache in front.
Storage: about 500 bytes per link is 50 GB a day, roughly 18 TB a year. More than one machine should hold for long, so plan to shard by code.
Codes: 6 base-62 characters give 5,600 crore codes, gone in about 18 months at this rate. 7 characters give 3.5 lakh crore, enough for decades.
Link: `code`, `long_url`, `created_by`, `created_at`, `expires_at`.
Click: `code`, `at`, `country`, `device` (written to a stream, counted later).

body.label: API
body.say: Two calls. POST to links with the long URL, and optionally a custom alias and an expiry, returns the short link. GET on the code answers with a 302 redirect to the long URL, or 404 if the code doesn't exist or has expired.

body.cap: Creating a link: the links API turns its next ID into a code, stores `code → URL` and returns `zot.to/2Bi`. Opening one, a hundred times more often: the redirect service checks Redis, falls back to the database on a miss, answers 302, and drops a click event into a stream for analytics.

body.x: Creating and opening are separate services because they scale differently: a few servers create links, many more answer redirects. Both use the same database, keyed by the code, so a redirect is one lookup by primary key.

body.name: First try
body.what: Hash the long URL (say MD5) and keep the first 7 characters.
body.use: No coordination: any server can make a code alone, and the same URL always gets the same code.
body.avoid: Two different URLs can share those 7 characters. You must check the database and retry on a clash, and the checks grow as the table fills.
body.ex: Two restaurants' offer pages happen to start with the same hash prefix; the second one silently gets the first one's code unless you check.
body.like: Naming children by the first letters of their surname: fine until two families share one.

body.name: Better
body.what: A single counter gives every new link the next number, written in base 62.
body.use: Codes never clash, and they're as short as possible.
body.avoid: Every create waits on one counter, a single point of failure. And codes are guessable in order: anyone can walk through `zot.to/2Bi`, `2Bj`, `2Bk`.
body.like: Token numbers at a bank counter: never two the same, but one machine prints them all.

body.name: Best
body.what: Each links server reserves a block of 1,000 numbers from the counter and hands them out from memory. If a server dies, the rest of its block is simply skipped.
body.use: No clashes, one counter call per 1,000 links, and servers keep working briefly if the counter is down.
body.avoid: Codes are still in order within a block. If guessable links matter (private documents), scramble the number first with a reversible shuffle, or add random characters.
body.like: Each bank counter gets its own roll of tokens.

body.cap: The counter hands each links server a block of 1,000 IDs; each turns its next ID into base 62. Server A's 10,000 becomes `2Bi`, server B's 11,157 becomes `2TX`. No two servers can produce the same code.

body.x: Custom aliases (`biryani50`) skip the counter: insert the alias as the code and let the database's unique key reject a duplicate, then ask the user to pick another. Keep aliases out of the counter's way too: if someone takes `2Bj`, the counter will hand out `2Bj` later and hit the same key. Require aliases of 8 characters or more, a length the counter won't reach for decades, or one with a `-`, which base 62 never uses.
Fast redirects at 3.5 lakh a second

items: Index: the code is the primary key, so even without a cache a lookup is about a millisecond. Fine for a start, not for 3.5 lakh a second on one database.

Cache: most clicks are on links made in the last few days. Keeping the hottest 20% of a day's links in Redis is about 10 GB, and most redirects never reach the database. Cache-aside with a TTL, as in the Caches article.

Edge: put the redirect behind a CDN that caches the 302 for a short time, so a link blasted in a crore SMS is answered near the customer. You lose per-click counting at the edge unless the CDN reports it.

body.x: A 301 tells the browser the move is permanent, so next time it skips you entirely: less load, but you never see those clicks and can't change or expire the link. A 302 sends every open through you: more load, but accurate click counts and the freedom to change where a link goes. Zotato's marketing team wants the counts, so it's 302, with caching to carry the load.

items: Shard the links table by code (hash of the code), since every redirect looks up exactly one code. See the Sharding article.

Replicate each shard; redirects can read from replicas, because a link that's a few hundred milliseconds old is rarely opened that fast. If a replica says a code doesn't exist, ask the primary before answering 404, and cache a 404 for seconds at most, so a brand-new link isn't stuck broken.
Expired links: don't delete them on the hot path. A nightly job removes them, and the redirect checks `expires_at` before answering.
Rate-limit link creation per account, so nobody makes millions of codes.
Check long URLs against a list of known malware and phishing sites before creating a link, and let people report bad links.
Never redirect to `javascript:` or other non-web schemes.
Junior / mid: the two calls, a database keyed by code, a working way to make codes (a counter is fine), and a cache once the read numbers come up.
Senior: the read-heavy numbers early, blocks of IDs or another clash-free scheme with its trade-offs, 301 vs 302 with a reason, sharding by code.
Lead: what happens when the counter or a shard is down, guessable codes, abuse, the edge cache vs click counting trade-off, and keeping it simple.
"The same long URL is shortened twice: same code?" Optional: keep an index on `long_url` per account and return the existing code, at the cost of one more lookup per create.

"Can a custom alias clash with a generated code?" Yes, if they share a format: an alias `2Bj` is a code the counter will reach. Give them separate spaces: aliases of 8 or more characters, or with a `-`.
"How do you count clicks without slowing redirects?" Write a click event to a stream (Kafka) and count in a separate consumer; the redirect never waits for it.
"What if Redis goes down?" Redirects fall through to the database replicas; size them for a cold cache at the busiest hour, as in the cache-restart challenge.
"Links in two regions?" Give each region its own range of IDs, so codes stay unique without talking across regions.

body.x: The same flood in the Lab: a promo SMS at 8 pm sends 30,000 taps a second at short links for 15 minutes. Keep redirects up without paying for a database that size.

practice.brief: The tests send redirects and new links in the mix the article works out: about 99 redirects for every new link. Every redirect makes one lookup; a cache in front of the database answers 9 in 10 of them. Your Clients' own rate is ignored: each test sends its own traffic.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 20,000 requests a second for an hour at 3 pm. Redirects must stay fast.

checks.label: Every redirect looks the short code up in a store built for lookups by key

tests.name: The evening peak
tests.desc: 35,000 requests a second for an hour at 8 pm, the busiest hour of the day.

checks.label: Every link is stored in a database

tests.name: A promo SMS at 8 pm
tests.desc: Zotato texts a link to 10 crore phones: for 15 minutes at 8 pm traffic jumps to 60,000 a second, five times the rest of the evening. New servers take 4 minutes to boot.

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the evening peak, the busiest group of servers crashes and is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of redirects still work
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the evening peak the database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of redirects still work
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A day of normal traffic (20,000 a second) on your design. Over-buying is a failure too.

fr.label: Create a short link from a long URL
Redirect: opening the short link sends you to the long URL

est.label: Redirects a second at peak
est.how: 100 opens per link → 1.2 lakh a second on average, about 3× that at peak

decisions.q: How do you make short codes that never collide?
options: A counter handed out in blocks to each server, written in base 62
Hash the long URL and keep the first 7 characters
Use the database row id as it is
decisions.why: Blocks of a counter give every server unique numbers without asking anyone per request, and base 62 keeps them short. A hash can collide and needs a check and retry; a raw id is long and shows how many links exist.

decisions.q: Which redirect does the short link send?
options: 302 (temporary): every click comes back to us, so we can count it and change or expire the link
301 (permanent): browsers remember it and stop asking us
decisions.why: A 301 saves traffic, but browsers stop asking, so click counts, edits and expiry stop working. Shorteners that count clicks use 302.

options: The database, with an index on the code
A cache in front of the store: a few popular links get most clicks
decisions.why: Clicks follow a steep curve: a small set of links gets most of them, so a cache answers most redirects and the store sees only the misses.

hints.x: Two things people do: make a short link (rare) and open one (constant). Which extras do marketing tools always ask for?
Start from 10 crore new links a day. Divide by 86,400 for writes a second, then multiply by opens per link for reads.
One call creates a link and returns it. The other is the short link itself: a GET on the code that answers with a redirect.
About 99 of every 100 requests are redirects that read the same popular links. What can answer repeated reads without touching the database?
Put a Cache between the servers and the database. At 90% hits only a tenth of the lookups reach the database.
For the promo test, new servers arrive too late (4 minutes). Keep enough servers running before 8 pm, or the spike crashes them.
Failures: two server groups behind the load balancer, and a database with Multi-AZ on, so a crash doesn't take every redirect down.

wrong.name: No cache
wrong.why: Every redirect reads the database, which can't take 35,000 lookups a second.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes every redirect fails for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes and every cache miss fails.

wrong.name: Sized for the average only
wrong.why: Fine at 35,000 a second, but the 60,000 spike crashes the servers before autoscaling helps.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.
